To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) cortical neuronal progenitors can be produced from human induced pluripotent cells and (2) these cells can be implanted into the stroke-dam-aged cerebral cortex and improve behavioural function.

we show that human induced pluripotent cells can be differentiated in vitro to cortical neuronal progenitor cells that can be converted to mature neurons and improve neurological function after transplantation into the injured rat cortex.
human induced pluripotent cells can be converted into neurons of a cortical phenotype that survive and improve functional recovery after transplantation in an animal model of stroke.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a stem cell therapy for stroke.

the generation of patient-specific induced pluripotent neural stem cells and their conversion to functional neurons, which may be used for transplantation to restore function after neurological injury.
the development and use of induced pluripotent cells for cell-based therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we have shown for the first time that human induced pluripotent cells can be differentiated into neurons, which survive and improve functional outcome after transplantation into a rat stroke model, although the mechanisms of the observed behavioural improvement are not clear at this stage.

the cortical fated cells, but not the non-fated cells, show the following characteristics: (1) less proliferation, (2) more efficient conversion to neurons, (3) more axonal projections, (4) pyramidal morphology, (5) TBR1 expression, and (6) electrophysiological functionality.

we have demonstrated the feasibility of using human induced pluripotent cells as a source of neurons for transplantation in stroke, but that the mechanisms by which the cells improve function remain to be elucidated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

human induced pluripotent cell-derived cortical progenitors can be generated in vitro and that these cells can be converted into functional neurons after transplantation into the adult stroke-damaged cerebral cortex, leading to functional recovery.

human induced pluripotent skin cells, when differentiated in vitro to neuroepithelial cells, can be converted into functional cortical neurons, which survive and improve functional recovery when transplanted into the stroke-injured cortex.

we have developed a new strategy for cell-based therapy of stroke by using human induced pluripotent skin-derived cells, which are differentiated to cortical neuronal precursors, and implanted into the damaged cortex of rats.
The main takeaway from our work is that
human induced pluripotent cells can be converted into cortical neuronal progenitors and that these progenitors can be transplanted into stroke-injured brain and improve neurological function.
the cortical progenitors derived from human induced pluripotent cells are able to integrate in the host circuitry and to improve functional recovery after stroke.
